title: Book Twelve (1812) — Chapter 7
paragraphs: The dreadful news of the battle of Borodino reached Voronezh in the middle of September, with word of our killed and wounded and, worse still, of the loss of Moscow. Princess Mary had learned of her brother's wound only from the Gazette and had no definite news of him. She was getting ready (so Nicholas heard; he hadn't seen her again himself) to set off in search of Prince Andrew.

News of the battle of Borodino and the abandonment of Moscow did not throw Rostov into despair, anger, a thirst for vengeance or anything of the kind. Instead, everything in Voronezh suddenly struck him as dull and tiresome, and he felt a vague shame and awkwardness. The conversations he overheard seemed insincere. He didn't know how to judge all these events and felt that only in the regiment would things become clear to him again. He hurried to finish buying the horses, and kept losing his temper for no reason with his servant and the squadron quartermaster.

A few days before he left, a special thanksgiving service for the Russian victory was held in the cathedral, and Nicholas attended. He stood a little behind the governor and kept a properly military bearing through the service while his mind wandered over all sorts of subjects. When it ended, the governor's wife beckoned him over.
"Have you seen the princess?" she asked, nodding toward a lady who stood on the opposite side, beyond the choir.

Nicholas knew Princess Mary at once, less from the profile he could see under her bonnet than from the rush of concern, shyness and pity that came over him. Princess Mary, plainly lost in her thoughts, was crossing herself for the last time before leaving the church.

Nicholas looked at her face in surprise. It was the face he had seen before, with the same look of refined inner spiritual effort, yet now it was lit up quite differently. It showed a touching mixture of sorrow, prayer and hope. As had happened before when she was near, Nicholas went up to her without waiting for the governor's wife to prompt him, and without asking himself whether it was proper to speak to her here in church. He told her he had heard of her trouble and sympathized with his whole soul. The moment she heard his voice a bright glow came into her face, lighting up her sorrow and her joy together.
"There's one thing I wanted to tell you, Princess," said Rostov. "If your brother, Prince Andrew Nikolaevich, were no longer alive, the Gazette would have announced it at once, since he's a colonel."
The princess looked at him without grasping what he said, but she was cheered by the regretful sympathy in his face.

"And I've known so many cases of a splinter wound" (the Gazette said it was a shell) "that either killed the man at once or turned out to be very slight," Nicholas went on. "We must hope for the best, and I'm sure..."
Princess Mary cut him short.

"Oh, that would be so dread..." she began, but she was too agitated to finish. She bowed her head with a movement as graceful as everything she did in his presence, gave him a grateful look, and went out after her aunt.

That evening Nicholas didn't go out. He stayed home to settle some accounts with the horse dealers. When he finished, it was too late to go anywhere and still too early for bed, and for a long time he paced the room, thinking over his life, which he rarely did.

Princess Mary had made a pleasant impression on him when he met her in Smolensk province. He had come across her in such exceptional circumstances, and his mother had once mentioned her as a good match, so he had paid her particular attention. When he met her again in Voronezh, the impression was not merely pleasing but strong. He had been struck by the unusual moral beauty he saw in her then. Yet he was about to leave, and it hadn't occurred to him to regret that he was giving up chances of seeing her. But that day's meeting in church, he felt, had gone deeper than was good for his peace of mind. That pale, sad, refined face, that radiant look, those gentle graceful gestures, and above all the deep tender sorrow in every feature of her face stirred him and drew out his sympathy. In men, Rostov couldn't stand the sign of a higher spiritual life (that was why he disliked Prince Andrew), and he scornfully called it philosophy and dreaminess. But in Princess Mary, that very sorrow, which showed the depth of a whole spiritual world foreign to him, was an irresistible attraction.

"She must be a wonderful woman. A real angel!" he said to himself. "Why am I not free? Why did I rush into things with Sonya?" And he couldn't help comparing the two: the lack of spirituality in one and the abundance of it in the other, a spirituality he lacked himself and therefore valued most highly. He tried to picture what would happen if he were free: how he would propose to her and how she would become his wife. But no, he couldn't imagine it. He felt awed, and no clear picture came to his mind. Long ago he had pictured a future with Sonya, and it was all clear and simple just because it had been thought through and he knew everything there was to know about Sonya. But a future with Princess Mary was impossible to picture, because he didn't understand her; he simply loved her.
Daydreams about Sonya had had something merry and playful in them, but dreaming of Princess Mary was always difficult and a little frightening.

"How she prayed!" he thought. "You could see her whole soul was in her prayer. Yes, that's the prayer that moves mountains, and I'm sure hers will be answered. Why don't I pray for what I want?" he suddenly thought. "What do I want? To be free, to be released from Sonya... She was right," he thought, remembering what the governor's wife had said: "Nothing but misfortune can come of marrying Sonya. Muddles, grief for Mamma... business difficulties... muddles, terrible muddles! Besides, I don't love her, not as I should. Oh, God! Release me from this dreadful, inextricable position!" he suddenly began to pray. "Yes, prayer can move mountains, but you have to have faith. You can't pray the way Natasha and I did as children, asking that the snow turn into sugar and then running out into the yard to see whether it had. No, I'm not praying for trifles now," he thought, and he put his pipe down in a corner, folded his hands and stood in front of the icon. Softened by his memories of Princess Mary, he began to pray as he hadn't for a long time. There were tears in his eyes and in his throat when the door opened and Lavrushka came in with some papers.
"Blockhead! Why do you come in without being called?" cried Nicholas, quickly changing his pose.
"From the governor," said Lavrushka in a sleepy voice. "A courier has arrived, and there's a letter for you."
"Well, all right, thanks. You can go!"

Nicholas took the two letters, one from his mother and the other from Sonya. He knew them by the handwriting and opened Sonya's first. He had read only a few lines when he turned pale, and his eyes opened wide with fear and joy.
"No, it's not possible!" he cried aloud.

He couldn't sit still. He paced the room with the letter in his hand, reading it. He ran his eye over it, then read it again, and again, and then he stopped in the middle of the room, shrugged, spread out his hands, and stood with his mouth wide open and his eyes fixed. What he had just been praying for, confident that God would hear him, had come to pass. Yet Nicholas was as astonished as if it were something extraordinary and unexpected. It was as if the very speed with which it had happened proved that it hadn't come from the God he had prayed to, but from some ordinary coincidence.

This unexpected letter from Sonya, which seemed to Nicholas entirely of her own free will, freed him from the knot that bound him, from which there had seemed no escape. She wrote that the latest misfortunes, the loss of almost all the Rostovs' Moscow property, and the countess' repeated wish that Nicholas marry Princess Bolkonskaya, together with his silence and coldness of late, had all led her to decide to release him from his promise and set him completely free.

It would be too painful for me to think that I might cause sorrow or discord in the family that has been so good to me (she wrote), and my love has no aim but the happiness of those I love. So, Nicholas, I beg you to consider yourself free, and to be sure that, in spite of everything, no one can love you more than does
Your Sonya

Both letters were written from Troitsa. The other, from the countess, described their last days in Moscow, their departure, the fire and the destruction of all their property. In it the countess also mentioned that Prince Andrew was among the wounded traveling with them. His condition was very critical, but the doctor said there was now more hope. Sonya and Natasha were nursing him.

Next day Nicholas took his mother's letter and went to see Princess Mary. Neither of them said a word about what "Natasha nursing him" might mean, but thanks to this letter Nicholas suddenly became almost as close to the princess as if they were relations.
The following day he saw Princess Mary off on her journey to Yaroslavl, and a few days later he left to rejoin his regiment.
